papers.title: 2,234 attempts to harmonize a multi-platform B-cell lymphoma bulk transcriptomic dataset: ComBat is superior by cross-batch prediction quality
papers.abstract: Background. Cross-platform transcriptomic harmonization benchmarks rely on individual success metric each: correlation with a reference profile, classifier accuracy, or a composite imported from single-cell integration. We found no published study that computes multiple orthogonal metric classes over one set of harmonization approaches and measures overlapping between the best approaches by these metrics. Methods. We used the 2,234 approaches of the recent real-world benchmark on 7,174 B-cell lymphoma transcriptomes. They combine 31 harmonization methods, 14 batch-removal strategies, three imputations and two post-removal settings. We assigned its 87 polarity-adjusted scoring metrics, out of 344 registered, to five classes (global, local, distributional, structural and composite) and added three biology-facing classes: within-cohort marker correlation (L), cross-batch rank agreement of a marker panel (M), and leave-one-batch-out (LOBO) prediction of lymphoma subtypes and normal B cells (N). Each class resulted in top 112 approaches (5%), and we measured overlap by the Jaccard index. Results. Harmonization methods of high harshness such as quantile normalization matched different batches to the same shape of distribution but were inferior by local and global metrics. Local and composite metrics resulted in the largest overlap of best approaches (71 shared). Classes L and M, M and N shared no approach, whereas L and N shared one approach without harmonization under the rare-batches-removed strategy, and all three overlaps were significantly below the random expectation. Class N resulted in the ComBat family in 84 of its 112 places. Class M elected only 10_mnn and 12_scanorama, methods that completely corrupted biology by correlation. Conclusions. Best transcriptomic harmonization approach is highly contingent on the quality metrics used, with metric classes trade-offing between each other. We provide a six-step recipe for metric classes, their thresholds and the cross-batch tests for selecting the best approaches.

papers.title: Multimodal phenotyping reveals plant-food-related dietary information in serum Raman spectra of community-dwelling Japanese adults
papers.abstract: Healthy dietary patterns are associated with long-term health, but diet-quality scores do not reveal how habitual dietary information is represented in human biological phenotypes. Here we linked habitual dietary assessment with preceding health records and contemporaneous clinical chemistry, serum metabolomics and serum Raman spectra in community-dwelling Japanese adults. Higher diet quality corresponded to a more favorable preceding health profile, but did not define discrete states across contemporary multivariate phenotypes. Instead, specific dietary information was recoverable across these layers: Raman spectra provided predictive information complementary to clinical and metabolomic measurements for multiple dietary variables. Raman variation corresponding to {beta}-carotene equivalent could be traced to carotenoid-assigned bands and aligned with a broader plant-food-related dietary dimension. These findings show that habitual diet is represented not as a single biological state but through biologically traceable dietary dimensions distributed across complementary phenotypic layers.

papers.title: Optimization of Search and Acquisition Strategies for DSSO Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry using Protein Prospector and Touchstone.
papers.abstract: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) enables residue-level characterization of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) in both purified assemblies and complex biological systems. Cleavable crosslinkers such as DSSO are widely used to facilitate analysis of complex samples, yet there remains limited consensus on how best to leverage their properties in both acquisition and data analysis workflows. In part, this reflects differences in scoring, classification, and false discovery rate (FDR) estimation across analysis pipelines. Therefore, an integrated XL-MS data analysis pipeline that enables confident identification of MS-cleavable cross-linked peptides through improved scoring and rigorous FDR assessment is essential for systematically comparing and benchmarking workflows across different sample preparations. To this end, we implemented a new capability within the Protein Prospector search engine to improve MS2-based identification of MS-cleavable cross-linked peptides. Next, we developed Touchstone, a framework for re-scoring, classification, FDR-controlled summarization, and visualization of Prospector XL-MS search results. Using this approach, we evaluate the contributions of DSSO-specific fragmentation features and compare multiple acquisition strategies across datasets ranging from purified macromolecular assemblies to proteome-scale samples. We find that the primary advantage of DSSO arises from enhanced backbone fragmentation of both linked peptides, rather than from diagnostic ion formation, and that incorporating diagnostic ion pairs into MS2-based scoring or filtering does not improve identification performance. Benchmarking against established datasets shows that Prospector-Touchstone performs comparably to leading methods for non-cleavable crosslinkers and provides improved performance for DSSO analysis. We further compare acquisition strategies and find that for purified protein assemblies, MS2.stHCD characterizes more residue-pairs than ETD-based, MS3-based, and hybrid methods. In contrast, for proteome-scale XL-MS, MS3-based acquisition yields similar numbers of inter-protein PPIs with lower error rates despite reduced sampling depth. Together, these results highlight complementary strengths of MS2- and MS3-based workflows and provide practical guidance for MS-cleavable XL-MS experiments with varying sample complexities.

papers.title: Alpha Spatial: Language-guided prediction of single-cell spatial gene expression from histology
papers.abstract: Routine histology preserves tissue architecture but leaves its molecular organization largely unmeasured. Recovering this information requires learning across heterogeneous gene panels and constraining a biologically ill-posed morphology-to-expression mapping. Here we present Alpha Spatial (AS), a language-conditioned framework that predicts cell-level gene expression from histology while jointly learning from different tissues and panels. Matched biological context improved prediction over omitted context, whereas incompatible context reduced accuracy. Multi-tissue learning further improved breast-tissue prediction, and AS outperformed the evaluated methods while preserving molecular-state organization. In breast cancer, AS recovered POSTN-associated stromal programmes and HER2-associated molecular and spatial differences. Exploratory patient-level analyses identified a CXCL14-associated spatial state whose abundance was associated with non-response to trastuzumab-containing treatment and larger residual invasive tumours. These findings establish a framework for reusing heterogeneous molecular observations to investigate tissue organization and treatment-associated microenvironments in archived histology.

papers.title: A spatial topology atlas of type I myofibers in porcine skeletal muscle reveals local slow-oxidative niches associated with meat quality traits
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle metabolism and meat quality are usually interpreted through myofiber type composition, fiber size, and histochemical state. Whether the spatial topology of myofibers constitutes an independent phenotype layer remains poorly quantified. Here, using succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-stained cross-sectional images from multiple pig breeds and more than 40 skeletal muscle sites, we established a multiscale spatial phenotyping framework for type I myofibers. To enable scalable instance-level quantification, we developed an improved Mask R-CNN segmentation workflow, trained with SAM-assisted and manually corrected annotations, and optimized for dense, small, irregular, and variably stained muscle fibers. This framework captures single-fiber morphology and staining, local contact, connected-cluster architecture, diffusion-ring neighborhoods, and global tissue configuration. Type I myofiber abundance was separable from spatial organization capacity: some muscles formed stronger-than-expected local connectivity and clustering despite modest type I fiber abundance. Spatial transcriptomic integration further showed that slow-oxidative genes and functional modules were non-randomly organized and formed local high-expression domains in type I fiber-enriched, high-contact neighborhoods. Across muscle sites and breeds, skeletal muscles displayed distinguishable type I fiber spatial topology identities, which were remodeled by breed background in a muscle-specific manner. In samples with matched meat-quality measurements, spatial topology features improved the explanation of pH, meat color, conductivity, and intramuscular fat. These results suggest that skeletal muscle should be modeled as a spatially organized tissue system rather than a simple mixture of fiber types.

papers.title: Cellular proximity and conditional coordination in the colorectal and pancreatic tumor microenvironment: a patient-level analysis of multiplexed imaging
papers.abstract: Immune cells in the tumor microenvironment are organized, and in colorectal and pancreatic cancer their arrangement around the tumor epithelium carries prognostic information. Multiplexed tissue imaging records the position and phenotype of every cell in a section, and studies of such images now routinely report that two cell types are spatially associated. However, the summaries behind these reports answer different questions. A proximity statistic asks whether two cell types lie close together more often than expected by chance. A conditional network asks whether their local densities rise and fall together once the other cell types are held fixed. The two can disagree, because every cell type is abundant where tissue is cell-dense and because the images of one patient are repeated measurements of that patient. We asked how epithelial and immune cells are organized in two settings: colorectal cancer with a Crohn's-like reaction (CLR) or diffuse inflammatory infiltration (DII), in 140 CODEX images from 35 patients, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) against its precursor, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), in 207 multiplex immunofluorescence images from 141 patients. We developed a patient-level analysis that keeps proximity, recurrent local composition and conditional coordination as separate quantities, tests conditional organization as a function of local epithelial density within each section, checks before every conditional estimate that the two cell types are disjoint sets of cells observed together in enough images, and calibrates each conclusion by patient-label permutation, cellularity adjustment under two definitions, spatial-scale perturbation and fully nested leave-one-patient-out prediction. In colorectal cancer, the conditional association between epithelial and myeloid density turned negative with local epithelial density about four times faster in DII than in CLR (difference $-0.0553$ per quartile; 95% CI, $-0.0833$ to $-0.0273$; patient-label familywise $P=0.006$), with no accompanying difference in proximity. In the pancreas, cytotoxic and helper T cells were closer together in PDAC than in IPMN at every scale examined ($qleq0.023$), whereas their conditional association differed between the two diseases under only one of the two cellularity definitions. Recurrent neighborhoods carried the most patient-level information in colorectal cancer (AUC 0.794) and combined spatial features in the pancreas (AUC 0.771). Pancreatic epithelial--immune and regulatory T-cell quantities could not be estimated from these cores and are reported as such. The analysis is implemented in the R package spatialMIFtools, available at https://github.com/sagnikbhadury/spatialMIFtools.

papers.title: Constructed Negatives Shape the Evaluation of Sequence-Based Protein--Protein Interaction Models
papers.abstract: Many machine-learning tasks, including representation learning, rely on negative examples that are constructed rather than directly observed. This issue is especially important for protein--protein interaction (PPI) prediction, where experimentally established non-interactions are scarce. PPI models are therefore commonly trained and evaluated against sampled, unobserved protein pairs treated as negatives. We study how this construction affects model comparison. Keeping positives, protein-disjoint splits, class balance, and model selection fixed, we vary training and evaluation negatives independently across six constructions and four sequence-based models, three of which use protein language model (pLM) representations. Changing only the test negatives shifts AUPRC by up to 0.26, and the top-ranked architecture changes with the construction. Negatives matched to true partners in pLM representation space reduce all pLM-based models to near-chance performance, and shuffling partners within each class shows that the original pairing contributes little to AUROC. Constructed training negatives rarely outperform uniform sampling: on external data, they underperform it in 108 of 120 comparisons for the pLM-based models, with gains never exceeding 0.05 AUROC and losses up to 0.23. We release splits, negative-generation procedures, and evaluation code that allow training and evaluation negatives to be varied separately. Our results show that with constructed negatives, model comparisons are not just noisy but systematically sensitive to how negatives are defined, a methodological choice that is often left implicit.

papers.title: A public-data reproducibility benchmark of a 2.5-D U-Net with a slice-level topology term for type-B aortic dissection segmentation
papers.abstract: Background: Type-B aortic dissection requires separation of the true and false lumina in heterogeneous, anisotropic CTA. A topology term may reduce fragmentation, but its reproducibility must be tested under a fixed case split and independent native-grid evaluation. Methods: We used the public Graz type-B aortic dissection CTA collection (40 cases; CC BY 4.0) and froze a 28/6/6 case split for training, development, and held-out testing. A compact 2.5-D U-Net trained with cross-entropy plus multiclass Dice was compared with the identical model augmented by a fixed-weight (0.5) differentiable slice-level soft clDice term. Two training seeds were run for each arm. All 40 cases passed the NRRD audit; predictions for six held-out cases were restored to their native grids and scored with case-level 3-D voxel-grid Dice, voxel-grid morphological clDice, 6-connected component counts, physical-volume error, and 2,000-resample case-level paired bootstrap intervals. Results: With seed 20261007, topology-minus-baseline differences were -0.028 (95% CI -0.053 to -0.004) for true-lumen Dice, +0.032 (-0.006 to +0.096) for true-lumen voxel-grid clDice, +0.071 (+0.037 to +0.103) for false-lumen Dice, and +0.073 (+0.048 to +0.103) for false-lumen voxel-grid clDice. With seed 20261008, the corresponding differences were -0.040 (-0.065 to -0.018), +0.013 (-0.034 to +0.071), -0.099 (-0.187 to -0.004), and -0.058 (-0.124 to -0.001). Descriptive pooled means over 12 case rows per arm were true-lumen Dice 0.577 for topology versus 0.611 for baseline and false-lumen Dice 0.409 versus 0.422; these pooled rows are not independent cases. Conclusions: Under this fixed six-case test split, the corrected slice-level topology term did not produce a consistent benefit. True-lumen Dice was lower in both seeds, while false-lumen effects reversed direction between seeds; topology-clDice changes were small and/or interval-crossing. The benchmark supports an auditable failure-analysis workflow but does not support a general topology benefit, clinical use, external generalization, or a panvascular decision system.

papers.title: ExpertTwins: Auditable Long Horizon Scientific Panels through Grounded Expertise
papers.abstract: Multi-agent language-model systems increasingly assign roles to agents and let them deliberate. A role label, however, does not specify which evidence an agent can bring or which standard it applies before accepting a conclusion. Agents that read one another's outputs tend to converge. We present ExpertTwins, a framework in which each seat of a scientific panel is defined by an inspectable evidence policy. Discipline seats retrieve under field-specific queries, and scientist-associated seats retrieve from attributed publications and a citation-derived scholarly neighborhood. Private initial packets, structured exchange, cited-source disclosure, deterministic quotation checks, and peer source review turn deliberation into an auditable record, which we also render as interactive idea-flow maps. Scientist associations denote publication-grounded perspectives, not replicas or endorsements of named researchers. In a nine-seat, four-turn neuroblastoma panel, 438 of 439 claims passed all attached quotation checks, and seats withdrew or defended positions when challenged on their evidence. A ten-turn panel sustained evidence acquisition and differentiated recommendations without conversational collapse. Across six base models given byte-identical initial packets, four sustained 97.9-99.8% quotation grounding, and at least 91% on every turn, whereas Haiku 4.5 failed by paraphrase and GPT-5 mini by silence. Agreement among strong models fell from 31% of claims at turn one to 5% at turn four. With follow-up questions held fixed, it stayed at 28-33% through turn three and fell to 20% only at the closing turn. Stress runs showed the collapse guardrail escalating through its full intervention ladder when consensus was forced, but missing deference to one unusually strong seat. On idea-flow maps, the forced consensus appeared as parallel lanes of identical ideas, although quotation grounding and participation balance stayed at their maxima. We also reimplemented two close published systems and ran them on matched models, seats, and questions. A multi-persona debate cited only real records, yet none of its cited sentences carried a checkable quotation and it had no way to abstain. An author-memory fusion system ran only after its fact checker was split by seat to fit in context. Its fused answer kept about two-thirds of the fact-checked specialist claims, answered 36 of 60 question parts on which our seats had abstained, and showed the reader 19% of its agents' disagreements. In a computational pathology case study, six scientist-associated agents built distinct pipelines to predict MYCN amplification from whole-slide images. Across six base models, seat-by-model interaction explained 57% of internal variance, and internal rank poorly predicted external rank (r = 0.18 across 36 nominees). These results establish differentiated, source-traceable scientific reasoning as an operational capability and identify the base model as a parameter that must be reported with the protocol.

papers.title: DUMMEST: A simpler and faster model for frameshift-aware alignment of a DNA sequence to a protein family
papers.abstract: Motivation: We address the problem of aligning DNA sequences containing frameshift errors to protein profile hidden Markov models (pHMMs), a task relevant to annotating protein-coding regions in long-read genomic, metagenomic, and transcriptomic sequence data. Existing approaches either translate sequences across six reading frames, ignoring frameshifts, or rely on slow and unreliable error correction. BATH natively models frameshifts but uses a more complex architecture than conventional pHMMs. Results: We propose a simpler frameshift-aware pHMM based on DUMMER, incorporating modern heuristics, including GPU-accelerated MMseqs2 prefiltering. Evaluations on simulated and real long reads show that our method detects more alignments, with greater average alignment lengths, than non-frameshift-aware tools. Compared with BATH, our method achieves comparable sensitivity and alignment lengths, improved specificity under simulated sequencing artifacts, and is 2--12x faster depending on dataset. Availability and Implementation: Source code and container image are freely available for download at: https://github.com/bioinfodlsu/dummest

papers.title: Biological and technical spatial variation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics technologies enable the identification of spatially variable genes that can shed light on tissue structure and function. However, spatial variability of gene expression can be due not only to biological function but also technical artifact. We develop a model for spatially variable capture that forms part of a bursty transcription model, allowing us to distinguish biological variability from spatially variable technical noise. Our approach is implemented in a program called stipple, which we demonstrate can be useful for identifying and interpreting spatial gene expression variation from spatial transcriptomics assays.

papers.title: PatientPheX: A Full-Text Biomedical Corpus for Patient-Specific Phenotype Information Extraction
papers.abstract: Patient-specific phenotype information extraction identifiers and normalizes phenotype entities and links them with individual patients, supporting rare disease research and genotype-phenotype analysis. However, existing datasets rarely combine full-text biomedical content with detailed annotations of patients, phenotypes, related entities, and their associations. In this work, we present PatientPheX, a corpus for patient-specific phenotype information extraction comprising 200 full-text articles, primarily case reports and case series. The corpus provides mention annotations and normalization for seven biomedical entity types, together with explicit associations between patients and entities across sentences, paragraphs, and sections. Negated findings and composite phenotype mentions are also annotated. Corpus construction combines automated pre-annotation, large language model (LLM)-assisted verification, and manual review and adjudication. Benchmarks cover entity recognition and normalization and patient-phenotype association extraction using gold-standard and predicted entities. The overall document-level entity F1 was 86.95%, while phenotype F1 was 79.33%. The best relation extraction macro-F1 decreased from 84.14% with gold-standard entities to 54.98% with predicted entities, highlighting the combined challenges of phenotype extraction and patient attribution. PatientPheX provides a resource for developing and evaluating patient-centered information extraction methods and supports the construction of structured patient-level knowledge resources for phenotype-driven biomedical research.

papers.title: From Closed-Set Annotation to In-Context Discovery: Biologically Grounded LLMs for Cellular Profiling
papers.abstract: Tumour heterogeneity reflects both cellular identity (lineage) and state (active transcriptional programs), yet computational methods generally analyse these axes separately. We introduce CellScribe, a generative framework that conditions a pretrained language model on frozen single cell foundation model embeddings through AdaLN adapters, enabling one shared model to generate an ontology- grounded cell type or a quantified meta-program profile. Supervised multitask fine- tuning produces fine grained typing across hundreds of cell types and outperforms generative and retrieval baselines on meta-program identification under study-holdout evaluation. We further train the model with reinforcement learning, scoring its generations against cell ontology distance and meta-program agreement, so that they align with biological knowledge rather than token agreement. To identify new cell types not present in the supervised training data, we post-train the model to read several labelled example cells in a single context, each conditioning its own text span, and infer the type of a query cell through in-context learning. CellScribe thus unifies cell identity and state in one generative interface, grounds both in biological structure, and identifies cell types outside the supervised vocabulary.

papers.title: Comparison of Total X-Ray Energy Absorbed by Fibroglandular Tissue and its Mass Derived from Full Field Digital Mammography and Digital Breast Tomosynthesis
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether total x-ray energy absorbed by fibroglandular tissue and fibroglandular tissue mass derived from raw and clinical full field digital mammography (FFDM) images corresponded with the respective quantities derived from digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT). A total of 840 paired FFDM and DBT observations were analyzed separately for the craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) orientations. Total absorbed x-ray energy and fibroglandular tissue mass were calculated using an automated breast density detection method in conjunction with the recorded average glandular dose. Relationships between FFDM and DBT quantities were evaluated in the log-log domain using linear and quadratic models, with model performance assessed by R2, adjusted R2, mean squared error (MSE), chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, and residual analysis. Strong associations were observed between FFDM and respective DBT quantities. For raw FFDM, linear energy models produced R2 values of 0.734 and 0.901 for the CC and MLO views, respectively, while the corresponding mass models produced R2 values of 0.634 and 0.870. Inclusion of a quadratic term improved model performance modestly. For clinical FFDM, linear energy models produced R2 values of 0.854 and 0.919, while the corresponding mass models produced R2 values of 0.721 and 0.812. The first-order coefficients for the clinical-image energy models were approximately unity (0.99-1.05), and inclusion of the quadratic term produced negligible changes in model performance and residual distributions. The goodness-of-fit tests did not reject adequate fit for any model. Clinical FFDM images can therefore provide estimates of total absorbed x-ray energy and fibroglandular tissue mass that are strongly associated with corresponding quantities derived from DBT. The approximately unit first-order coefficients and minimal benefit from quadratic modeling support a simple linear log-log calibration for clinical FFDM. This approach may facilitate combining FFDM and DBT based data in larger retrospective and longitudinal studies of cumulative mammographic x-ray exposure. These findings demonstrate proof-of-concept internal consistency but do not establish absolute dosimetric accuracy.

papers.title: SVC: A Vision Transformer-based Spatially and Virtually Embedded Cell Model for Deciphering Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomic Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Subcellular transcript localization shapes gene regulation and cellular function, yet profiling it at scale remains difficult, limiting our ability to study subcellular heterogeneity across tissues and disease. Here, we present SVC, a Vision Transformer-based spatially and virtually embedded cell model that learns subcellular transcript organization within native tissue context directly from subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics. SVC represents each gene's subcellular localization as an image patch and uses other genes within the same cell as context, enabling subcellular contextual learning of spatial dependencies that govern intracellular organization. By integrating gene-function priors, cell morphology, spatial context, and, when available, cell identity, SVC captures unified, spatially grounded representations across genes and cells that connect subcellular organization to cellular state and tissue microenvironment. Across diverse subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, SVC accurately predicts cell-specific subcellular transcript localization and co-organization, generalizes across tissues and technical platforms, and supports subcellular imputation of unmeasured genes and in silico perturbation. Leveraging these capabilities, SVC highlights disease-associated patterns of intracellular transcript reorganization and spatially heterogeneous responses to gene perturbations. Beyond prediction, SVC reveals systematic variation in subcellular transcript organization associated with gene function, cellular states, and tissue microenvironments, uncovering de novo spatial biology that is not accessible by cell-level analysis. SVC's learned representations further transfer to cell- and tissue-level tasks, including cell-level expression imputation, cell clustering, and spatial domain detection. Together, SVC provides a general framework for modeling and interrogating subcellular transcript organization in situ, enabling scalable discovery of subcellular spatial biology.

papers.title: FERDINAND: An Open Framework for Download and AI-ready Preprocessing of IMPC 2D Radiographs
papers.abstract: The International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium (IMPC) maintains a large archive of whole-body dorsoventral radiographs. However, heterogeneity in file formats, metadata completeness, orientation, and image quality limits its reuse for large-scale quantitative analysis. We present FERDINAND (Framework for Extracting and Restructuring Distributed IMPC radiographs into a Normalised, AI-ready Navigable Dataset), an open framework for programmatic access, harmonisation, quality control, and curation of IMPC radiographs. FERDINAND combines metadata retrieval and local radiograph archiving with centre-aware preprocessing, automated exposure screening, orientation standardisation, and clustering-assisted visual curation. Applied to IMPC Data Release 24, FERDINAND organises 104,819 radiographs acquired between February 2012 and June 2025 across ten phenotyping centres and 6,306 single-gene knockout mouse lines, with semi-automated curation recorded for every image. As an independent validation of the harmonised output, a DeepLabCut-based bone-morphometry pipeline showed that FERDINAND-processed radiographs improve data efficiency for landmark detection: at reduced training-set sizes, they achieve better performance than original radiographs and require fewer manual annotations to reach a given level of quality. FERDINAND provides a reproducible foundation for artificial intelligence (AI)-ready analysis and scalable quantitative phenotyping of heterogeneous IMPC and comparable radiograph resources. The complete FERDINAND source code is openly available on GitHub.

papers.title: Evidence-resolved benchmarks separate biological context recognition from direct-partner specificity in protein interaction models
papers.abstract: Sequence-based models enable scalable protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction, but whether high scores identify direct physical partners or broader biological compatibility remains unclear. Here we show that biological-context recognition and direct-partner specificity are separable prediction capabilities. We introduce ProtNegDB (http://protnegdb.bjmu.edu.cn/), an evidence-resolved resource distinguishing experimentally supported non-binding from coordinate-verified noncontact within PDB biological assemblies. Using context-matched benchmarks, we find that five sequence-based predictors show limited ability to distinguish direct partners from noncontacting members of the same assembly, whereas PLM-Interact readily ranks both above unrelated proteins. Representation analyses reveal that adaptation to PPI prediction can strengthen biological-context encoding without yielding transferable direct-contact specificity. AlphaFold3 shows greater, though still incomplete, direct-partner resolution, suggesting that explicit multimer modeling can help refine partner specificity. In PLM-Interact, negatives defined by reconstituted direct-binding, cellular binary/proximity and co-complex assays occupy distinct score regimes. Across independent datasets and multiple models, experimental direct non-binding and assembly noncontact further show reproducible, model-dependent scoring patterns. High sequence-based PPI scores should not be interpreted as direct-interface probabilities. Mechanistically interpretable evaluation instead requires explicit consideration of interaction-evidence semantics and partner specificity.

papers.title: Limits of marker information transfer]{Limits of marker information transfer in cross-panel cytometry imputation
papers.abstract: Marker imputation can bridge cytometry datasets acquired with different panels and platforms. Its validity depends on whether common markers retain information about unmeasured target markers and whether those relationships transfer across assay contexts. We evaluated these limits in two paired flow cytometry-CyTOF cohorts comprising 134 patients and 257 specimens. A patient-held-out framework distinguished within-platform same-cell reconstruction from cross-platform distribution translation without cell correspondence. We compared conventional machine-learning and deep generative estimators with median imputation and used permutation controls to estimate the contributions of patient matching and source-exclusive markers. Evaluation covered marker values, specimen distributions, phenotype utility, and directional predictive relationships among markers. Within platforms, exact k-nearest neighbors reduced mean absolute error by 12.8-35.0% relative to median imputation. However, the median-based reconstructions were contracted, with a median ratio of predicted to observed interquartile range below 1 in every context and evaluable population. Patient matching improved cross-platform distribution recovery, whereas adding source-exclusive markers or higher-capacity estimators did not consistently produce net gains. In the independently annotated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cohort, reconstructed markers largely preserved broad-lineage classification but did not recover fine-phenotype information available through direct measurement. In AML-CyTOF, the measured full panel outperformed the reconstructed representation by 10.25 percentage points for fine phenotypes. Predictive relationships among markers were context-specific. Most targets were better explained by several markers than by one. Marker selection based on these relationships showed a trade-off between panel size and pairwise coverage. Paired samples and imputation can therefore connect selected marker distributions across panels but should not be treated as substitutes for direct measurement. Cross-panel cytometry should be evaluated with patient-held-out tests matched to the resolution of available ground truth and the intended downstream use.

papers.title: Why 627 BindCraft2 trajectories produced zero binders
papers.abstract: De novo protein-binder design with deep-learning pipelines such as BindCraft2 has been reported to deliver experimental success rates of 10-100% against well-structured targets. Here we report the opposite tail: two BindCraft2 (v1.0.3) cyclic-peptide campaigns targeting the shallow K81 lactylation epitope of human lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) produced zero accepted designs from 627 trajectories. Retrospective analysis of the campaign artifacts shows that 97% of trajectories were rejected at the first ("screen") stage by a single confidence gate (binder pLDDT < 0.60), not because the interface failed to form: the interface metric i_pTM reached 0.69 and the target was confidently folded (pTM = 0.90). Critically, the mid-project decision to disable the "lysine trick" (forced_targeting) was backwards -- that feature moved 17 trajectories past the screen versus 1 without it, and raised interface confidence. We document two preset/metric mismatches that set a macrocycle campaign up to fail regardless of budget: a screen-stage pLDDT gate calibrated for globular binders, and a binder_contacts loss that is degenerate for short peptides. We describe the exact artifacts BindCraft2 writes and distill them into a reusable post-mortem protocol, and we include a complete how-to-use-BindCraft2 guide so the failure analysis also serves as a tutorial.

papers.title: Bayesian phylogenetics with incomplete lineage tracing data
papers.abstract: Single-cell lineage tracing is rapidly emerging as a powerful method to track the dynamics of cell populations through time. Specifically, CRISPR-Cas9-based dynamic lineage tracing methods generate high-resolution data with the potential to investigate increasingly complex biological processes. However, single-cell readouts are inherently lossy, resulting in significant sparsity in lineage barcode alignments. Here, we present a mechanistic model of barcode loss implemented in the Bayesian framework BEAST 2, enabling phylogenetic inference from sparse datasets without the need for data filtering. Through simulations, we find that incorporating a mechanistic model of loss improves accuracy across all estimates in phylogenetic analyses by enabling previously unusable data to contribute to the inference. We further demonstrate the model's utility across two datasets: one from a monoclonal cell culture and another from murine gastruloids. Consistent with our simulation findings, applying our model to these datasets recovers higher growth rates than workflows relying on standard data filtering, confirming that such filtering can lead to an underestimation of population expansion. Crucially, we demonstrate that our framework enables inference even from datasets whose sparsity previously prevented analysis, providing a robust foundation for extracting biological insights from lineage tracing experiments.

papers.title: Decomposing scanner batch effects and their impact on pathology foundation models
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (PFMs) are expected to represent the same tissue in the same way on any scanner, but their embeddings still carry scanner signals. Scanner-related image differences and the scanner sensitivity of PFMs have each been described. How tissue-dependent changes in color and spatial frequency relate to shifts in PFM representations, and what this means for correction, is less understood. We imaged 103 slides from 37 normal tissue types on six scanners (PanNormal; 95,780 matched locations) and used the real paired images as targets. We used the public PLISM dataset for external validation. First, we decomposed scanner differences into image properties. Color and spatial frequency changed together, by amounts that depended on tissue type. Second, corrections that matched these measured properties brought images closer to the target more reliably than representations. Pix2Pix reduced the image residual by 69% but increased UNI distance to the target by 27%. The same frequency matching helped one scanner and hurt another. Probes still distinguished corrected from real target embeddings after every correction. Third, changing one frequency band at a time showed that PFMs differ in how strongly each band moves them and whether it moves them toward the target. Across eight PFMs pretrained on whole-slide image tiles, the models that moved least under these small changes were the most robust to real scanner differences (Spearman {rho}=-0.90). Aligning images and aligning representations are therefore different goals. The gap between them depends on scanner, tissue, and model.

papers.title: DiffRhyShiny: A Benchmarking-Informed Platform for Differential Rhythmicity Analysis with Dependence-Aware Evidence Integration
papers.abstract: Motivation: Differential rhythmicity analysis identifies condition-specific changes in biological oscillations, but diverse algorithmic assumptions complicate method selection. Furthermore, integrating complementary evidence across different tools while accounting for statistical dependence remains an unresolved challenge. Results: We benchmarked seven algorithms across diverse rhythmic scenarios, revealing that optimal selection depends heavily on specific biological variations and experimental designs. To overcome single-algorithm limitations, we introduced Kost's Method, a dependence-aware p-value integration approach. Building on this framework, we developed DiffRhyShiny, an interactive web platform that automates robust differential rhythmicity analysis, consensus evaluation, and visualization. Furthermore, we validated the platform's performance and statistical rigor using both extensive simulated scenarios and real-world transcriptomic datasets. Availability and implementation: DiffRhyShiny is freely available at https://omicsai.shinyapps.io/diffrhyshiny, with the latest source code at https://github.com/liuchuan111/diffrhyshiny. The code and data to reproduce all benchmarking results are archived on Figshare at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.33070100.

papers.title: DNA-LLM2Vec: Architecture-Aware Task-Conditioned Adaptation of Decoder DNA Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Decoder DNA foundation models pretrain with dense next-token prediction and scale to long sequences, but their representations are directional. This is a poor fit for genomic tasks that need sequence context both upstream and downstream of a locus. Bidirectional masked-language-model encoders supply this context, but they pretrain more sparsely and scale less easily to long windows. We introduce DNA-LLM2Vec, a staged decoder-to-encoder framework that opens bidirectional context, repairs the resulting mismatch with masked next-token prediction, and applies contrastive views encoding strand and positional invariance. We instantiate it on two architecturally distinct backbones, DNAGPT and HyenaDNA, and evaluate seven biological task families (grouped from GB, NT, GUE, and GUE+EPI) with frozen linear probing. The benefits of conversion are architecture-aware and task-conditioned rather than uniform. Crop-based positional contrastive learning helps most for the extended-context families (enhancer-promoter interaction and Virus-COVID), raising frozen Avg-EPI MCC to 27.5% for DNAGPT and 26.7% for HyenaDNA, whereas for shorter, local families the results depend on backbone and tokenisation. Beyond classification, bidirectional context and MNTP improve causal-eQTL variant-effect prediction specifically at distance, and a base-pair mutagenesis diagnostic shows that adaptation organises motif-aware contact structure while reverse-complement training imprints strand-consistent geometry, yet neither predicts the best downstream view. DNA-LLM2Vec therefore produces frozen bidirectional representations whose most effective adaptation view depends on the task structure and the backbone. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/semi-nothing/dna-llm2vec.

papers.title: NCI-Profiler: automated protein-ligand interaction detection and visualization
papers.abstract: Non-covalent interactions govern ligand binding specificity and affinity, but existing analysis tools cover a limited set of interaction types, treat metal coordination as a generic contact, and struggle to depict macrocyclic ligands such as heme or cobalamin, leaving comprehensive interaction analysis fragmented across multiple programs. We developed Non-Covalent Interaction Profiler (NCI-Profiler), a free web-based and command-line tool for automated detection and visualization of nine types of protein-ligand non-covalent interactions, including metal coordination and halogen-water-hydrogen (XWH) bridges. NCI-Profiler detects interactions directly from PDB or mmCIF coordinates using literature-derived geometric criteria, without manual structure preparation, and produces interactive 2D diagrams, an in-browser three-dimensional viewer, and downloadable 3D PyMOL sessions, together with structured output files. Its accuracy was validated against 85 literature-annotated complexes and directly compared against PLIP, an established interaction-detection tool, on the same dataset. NCI-Profiler achieved F1-scores of 92-100% for {pi}-{pi} stacking, metal coordination, and water bridges, and 77-83% for the remaining types except hydrophobic contacts (54.8%); it detected literature-confirmed interactions more completely than PLIP in five of nine categories and ran roughly twice as fast. Three case studies further show its expanded coverage can reveal binding-pocket growth vectors, explain structure-activity trends, and distinguish receptor-subtype selectivity. NCI-Profiler is freely available at https://ncip.khu.ac.kr.

papers.title: E3 Ligase Ligandalyzer: A Structure-First, Ligand-Centric Platform for E3 Ligase Recruiter Selection
papers.abstract: Here, we present E3 Ligase Ligandalyzer Version 1.0, a freely accessible, recruiter-centric web platform for comparative exploration of experimentally resolved E3 ligase-recruiter complexes. The locked Version 1.0 dataset spans 35 E3 ligases, 604 reconciled recruiter entities, and 1,372 active structure-specific recruiter instances across 685 experimentally resolved PDB structures. Recruiters are linked to normalized chemical representations and analyzed using cheminformatics and structure-based workflows to compute physicochemical descriptors, scaffold relationships, aligned binding-pocket views, and solvent-accessible surface area patterns relevant to linker attachment. The platform integrates recruiter-entity, recruiter-instance, scaffold, and ligase views, allowing users to compare experimentally grounded chemical and structural observations without imposing predictive rankings. The platform supports direct transition into downstream degrader-design workflows, including integration with PROTAC Builder (protacbuilder.com). E3 Ligase Ligandalyzer is freely available at https://e3ligandalyzer.com, and the associated code and dataset-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/schurerlab/E3-Ligandalyzer-Scripts.

papers.title: Computational Prediction of Recombinant Expression Efficiency for Industrial Enzymes: An Integrated Co-Translational Sequence Analysis Platform
papers.abstract: Industrial biocatalysis relies on the cost effective production of active enzymes in heterologous hosts, yet a substantial fraction of candidate sequences fails during recombinant expression because sequence-level determinants of translational efficiency are not captured by conventional codon optimization alone. Here we present an integrated computational platform for pre-clinical assessment of industrial enzyme expression potential that combines baseline sequence metrics with co-translational modeling of ribosome stalling, translation rhythm, codon harmonization, folding bottlenecks, solubility proxies, and proteolysis risk. The platform accepts DNA, protein, FASTA, and PDB inputs and returns interpretable expression risk assessments, component-level diagnostics, variant design proposals, and actionable engineering recommendations. Analyses are parameterized for industrial expression hosts (Escherichia coli, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Bacillus subtilis, and mammalian cells) and for native enzyme sources including Streptomyces, Bacillus, filamentous fungi, actinomycetes, and extremophiles. All analyses execute locally without dependence on external databases, enabling rapid and secure screening of proprietary enzyme candidates prior to gene synthesis and fermenter scale-up. We report three layers of preliminary validation on small cohorts: (i) a retrospective public industrial-enzyme ranking benchmark (n = 20; rank subset n = 10); (ii) calibration of the solubility module on held-out eSOL enzymes with quantitative experimental solubility; and (iii) an independent collaborator wet-lab construct set retained as a true external-test holdout and never used for model fitting (n = 38 labeled constructs). On the external holdout, solubility calls achieved accuracy 68.4% (95% CI 52.5 - 80.9%), sensitivity 56.5% (36.8 - 74.4%), specificity 86.7% (62.1 - 96.3%), balanced accuracy 71.6% (bootstrap 95% CI 57.4 - 84.4%), and MCC 0.43 (0.15 - 0.69). Sensitivity remains close to chance on this small set, whereas specificity is higher; intervals are wide and the evidence should be read as directional rather than definitive. A directional arginine-surface redesign example (SrMilN insoluble parent to SrMilN_SASAR partially soluble variant; incomplete rescue with multiple soluble bands) was recovered. These findings support preliminary screening utility and transparent experimental agreement, but do not constitute high-accuracy prediction of industrial fermenter titre. Offline EC-class heuristics are retained only as optional provisional labels and are not presented as a validated platform capability (agreement 3/20 = 15%, 95% CI 5.2 - 36%; chance for six classes is 16.7%).

papers.title: Protein novelty, sequence similarity, and negative sampling controls reveal benchmark specific discrimination in protein protein interactionprediction
papers.abstract: Protein protein interaction (PPI) predictors are often evaluated with random pair splits that permit proteins to recur across training and test sets, while constructed negative pairs can introduce a separate source of benchmark-specific signal. We reassessed the Guo yeast benchmark using a matched protein novelty curve, independently generated MMseqs2 sequence cluster controlled R3 variants, topology only controls, degree- and length matched putative negatives, handcrafted and frozen protein language model representations, multiple model configurations, seed analyses, and connected component aware inference. In the matched R1[->]R2[->]R3 comparison, AAC+CTD-MLP ROC-AUC declined from 0.697 for seen-seen pairs to 0.626 for one-unseen pairs and 0.587 for both-unseen pairs. Across independently regenerated cluster-disjoint R3 variants at 50%, 40%, 30%, and 20% MMseqs2 clustering thresholds, performance showed no consistent monotonic trend. Guo original-negative endpoints had lower positive-network degree than positive endpoints (mean 3.34 versus 6.72), and a degree-only logistic model reached ROC-AUC 0.962 on the original negatives but 0.502 on degree-matched negatives. We used degree-matched negatives consistently for R3 training and testing; six sequence based model configurations yielded ROC-AUC 0.493- 0.547; none showed corrected connected-component-aware evidence of above-chance discrimination. A PIPR multispecies analysis reproduced degree-associated label separation but also exposed cross-species pairing as an additional pooled cue. These results show that protein novelty, operational sequence cluster separation, and negative-set topology are distinct dimensions of PPI benchmark evaluation. The Guo result is benchmark-specific and should not be generalized to sequence-based PPI prediction or protein language models overall. The dataset and source code for the experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/morufwork/guoAudit.git.

papers.title: Revealing pan-cancer clonal niches of T cells from single-cell RNA sequencing using contrastive learning
papers.abstract: T-cell clonal organization is central to anti-tumor immunity, yet its functional characterization typically requires paired single-cell RNA and TCR sequencing (scRNA/TCR-seq). Existing multimodal methods integrate transcriptome and TCR information but are limited when TCR data are unavailable. Here we present CloneTrast, a supervised contrastive-learning framework that uses paired scRNA/TCR-seq during training to learn clonal-functional states from gene expression, while requiring only scRNA-seq at inference. Using paired scRNA/TCR-seq profiles from 2.6 million human T cells across 16 cancer types, CloneTrast identified distinct T-cell clonal niches not explained solely by TCR sequence similarity or conventional cell-state annotations. Among these, an NK-like T-cell niche enriched for tumor-blood shared TCRs was consistently associated with poor immunotherapy response at the pan-cancer level. Analysis of antigen-specific T-cell clones revealed that tumor-resident and blood-borne antigen-specific T cells were preferentially associated with distinct clonal niches. Overall, CloneTrast enables scalable and interpretable inference of clonal organization from single-cell transcriptomes.

papers.title: BCell-Epitope-Prediction: A local, reproducible pipeline for multi-epitope vaccine design: integration and structural validation against a panel of PDB antigen-antibody complexes
papers.abstract: Epitope-based subunit vaccine design requires chaining together heterogeneous analyses: B-cell antigenicity, topological accessibility, self-tolerance, allergenicity, T-helper/T-cytotoxic immunogenicity, and literature corroboration, historically scattered across separate, often web-only tools. This work presents a computational pipeline that integrates fourteen external tools across eight main phases, runs locally without network calls, and uses content-based self-caching. B-cell antigenicity is assessed via four engines (BepiPred-3.0, EpiDope, DiscoTope-3.0, and ScanNet), whose per-residue scores are fused into a single signal before thresholding. Validation used a panel of seventeen real antigen-antibody complexes from the Protein Data Bank spanning five pathogenic species, with ground truth from structural contact and independent literature verification. Fusing the four engines' scores, completed to a fixed candidate count, outperforms the best individual engine in F1 while reducing predicted residue volume. T-helper and T-cytotoxic immunogenicity are evaluated over each antigen's complete sequence, independently of the B-cell candidates. The final construct retains a B-cell epitope in 13 of 17 structures, and a T-cell block in 13 of 17 antigens, of which 6 match literature-documented epitopes and 2 more show partial correspondence.

papers.title: VesperFlow: An automated pipeline for decoding multisensor data from biologging tags
papers.abstract: Integrating multi-sensor data from biologging tags is key to understanding animal behavior, particularly in group-living species, where communication, movement, and spatial dynamics are closely linked. However, analyzing such data at scale is often hindered by proprietary binary formats or manual decoding workflows in existing software. We present VesperFlow, an open-source Python pipeline that automates the decoding of inertial measurement unit (IMU), audio, and GPS data from Vesper Wildlife tags. VesperFlow batch-processes large datasets from multiple individuals, synchronizes timestamps across sensors with sub-second precision, and removes hardware-induced artifacts such as spurious gyroscope spikes and audio pops. Outputs are exported as CSV and WAV files for direct use in common downstream analysis workflows. We validate the pipeline on field data from 10 ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta), showing that our pipeline reliably processes movement, vocal, and spatial data. By lowering technical barriers and automating processes, VesperFlow supports more scalable, multi-modal research on animal behavior. VesperFlow is freely available at https://github.com/dasilva98/vesperflow.
